opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started because I'm a fan. I'd been watching Simon and Mark for years, just for fun, and at some point it clicked that what they're doing on camera is incredibly rare: they're thinking out loud, for an hour or more, on a genuinely hard reasoning problem. And they're not just giving you the answer. They're showing you the false starts, the "oh wait, that can't be right," the moment where they spot some weird interaction between two constraints that unlocks the whole puzzle.

That's exactly the kind of data we don't really have for training reasoning models. Most of what's on the internet is the polished final product: the proof, the solution, the answer. You almost never see the messy process of how a human expert actually got there. These videos are thousands of hours of expert-level, step-by-step reasoning traces, narrated in natural language, on problems where you can verify the answer perfectly at the end.

And the variant Sudokus they solve are interesting because they're not ordinary Sudoku. Every puzzle has its own novel rules, so you can't just memorize a technique and grind it out. The setters design these "break-ins," clever insights you have to discover. So it's a really nice testbed for whether a model can find creative reasoning steps instead of brute-forcing a search. Current models, even the strong reasoning ones, still struggle a lot on the harder ones, which tells you there's real headroom there.

So it felt like a perfect combination: verifiable problems, real novelty, and a huge archive of humans demonstrating how to think through them. We were lucky the guys were enthusiastic about it too.

r001.rationale: The response favors narrated reasoning traces over polished answers for training reasoning models, but it does not identify them as a training source for AGI or describe them as thought processes behind text creation.

r002.rationale: It describes the videos as thousands of hours of expert, step-by-step Sudoku reasoning narrated in natural language, making them a source of human reasoning traces.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it started as a bit of an obsession of mine, honestly. I'd been watching Simon and Mark for years, long before I thought about it as data. And at some point it struck me that what you're watching in those videos is something you almost never get to see anywhere else, which is a human being reasoning out loud, in real time, for an hour or two, on a problem that's genuinely hard for them.

Most of the text we train on is the finished product. Someone had an insight, maybe they struggled for days, and then they wrote down the clean version. The struggle is gone. The dead ends are gone. All the little moments of "hmm, that can't be right, let me back up" have been edited out. But that's exactly the part we want models to learn, isn't it? Not the answer, but the process of getting there.

What Simon does is narrate everything. He says what he's noticing, why he thinks a particular digit might go somewhere, he tests a hypothesis, he realises it breaks something three boxes over, and he says so and undoes it. He'll spend twenty minutes on something and then go, "oh, of course," and you can see the whole structure of the problem suddenly reorganise in his head. And crucially, you can verify every step. Sudoku has a ground truth. So you have this rare combination of long-horizon, messy, honest reasoning traces that are also completely checkable.

The other thing I found compelling is that these puzzles are constructed. Setters design them around a specific idea, a particular break-in, and often the difficulty isn't computational at all, it's about finding the right way to look at the grid. That felt much closer to what we actually mean when we talk about reasoning than, say, a model grinding through a search. There's a lot of talk about chain of thought, and I just thought, here are thousands of hours of what really good chain of thought actually looks like, by someone who's a world-class solver, and nobody was treating it as data. So we did.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts polished finished text with the visible human struggle and reasoning that produced it, and says models should learn that process rather than only the answer.

r002.rationale: It describes Simon narrating detailed Sudoku reasoning, including hypotheses, mistakes, and corrections, and presents the videos as thousands of hours of usable reasoning traces.

astra-6.text:
What struck me was that you’re watching someone explain how they solve a problem, rather than just seeing the problem and the answer. They’ll say, “This digit can’t go here because that would force something over there,” and you can follow the deductions as they build on one another.

Sudoku also gives you a very constrained setting: the rules are clear, and you can check whether a deduction is valid. So you’ve got this combination of human explanations and a problem where correctness is testable. That seemed like a really interesting source of training data for reasoning—teaching a model how to make progress, rather than just what the completed grid looks like.

r001.rationale: The response favors explanations of how a person reasons through a problem over seeing only the problem and completed answer, and describes them as training data for teaching reasoning.

r002.rationale: It describes following spoken Sudoku deductions as they build and presents those explanations as a source of reasoning training data; the preceding context identifies the videos as Cracking the Cryptic’s.

sol-6.1.text:
What struck me was that you don’t just get a puzzle and its solution—you get someone explaining how they get there. They’ll notice a constraint, follow an idea for a bit, realise it doesn’t work, and come back to something else. That process is much closer to what we want from a reasoning system than simply producing the right answer.

And Sudoku gives you this lovely, self-contained setting where you can check whether a deduction is valid. So you’ve got rich explanations of how to make progress, alongside rules that let you verify that progress. That combination seemed really valuable.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the solver’s reasoning process, including trying and abandoning ideas, with simply giving the answer, and says that process is closer to what a reasoning system needs. The question supplies the training-data context.

r002.rationale: It describes someone explaining how they solve Sudoku, calls those explanations rich, and says they provide valuable reasoning information alongside verifiable rules.
